fatal_errors: The proposed material family is a generic refractory HEA rather than the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA with FCC and B2 phases.

The hypothesis changes the controlling variable from aging temperature to aging time and therefore does not reconstruct the approximately 550–750 °C brittle window or the 600 °C minimum and 750 °C recovery.
It attributes recovery to precipitate coarsening and loss of coherency instead of reduced L12 ordering and formation of ductile transition zones along B2/FCC phase boundaries.
It omits the coupled role of near-Ni3Al L12 ordering, elevated antiphase-boundary energy, planar slip, and stress concentration at jagged B2/FCC boundary tips.
No cited evidence establishes the required prior existence or aging evolution of B2/L12 chemical ordering in the proposed W-Ta-Mo-Nb-V system.
The cited coherent-nanoprecipitate evidence reports improved dislocation transmission and ductility, not ordering-induced embrittlement, so it does not support the stated mechanism.
explanation: The response correctly focuses on multiphase high-entropy alloys, tensile ductility, thermal aging, chemical ordering, and a possible ductile-brittle-ductile trajectory. However, it reconstructs a substantially different alloy and mechanism. The target concerns an as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic FCC+B2 alloy whose ductility varies non-monotonically with aging temperature because enhanced L12 ordering and jagged phase boundaries jointly produce planar-slip localization and crack initiation near 600 °C, followed by recovery near 750 °C. The generated hypothesis instead proposes coherent nanoprecipitate formation and subsequent coarsening in an unspecified RHEA, with non-monotonicity primarily as a function of aging time. Its boundary conditions are qualitative and do not identify the target temperature limits. The experiment can test the alternative time-dependent hypothesis, but it does not directly examine dislocation pile-ups or crack initiation at jagged phase-boundary tips, nor exclude impurity-segregation-based intergranular embrittlement. Most importantly, the cited evidence does not validate the assumed ordered precipitates or the claimed embrittlement/coarsening sequence in the selected alloys.
